newsitem.title: ITALY: Milan bomb blast raises scare ahead of Italy vote.
newsitem.headline: Milan bomb blast raises scare ahead of Italy vote.

text.p: A bomb blast damaged Milan city hall on Friday just three days before local elections in which the post of mayor of Italy's financial capital will be the biggest prize.
The dawn explosion blew a hole in the back wall of the city hall and caused some damage to the council chamber itself as well as shattering windows in adjacent buildings, police said.
No one was injured but Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano said the device, consisting of gunpowder and bolts packed into a steel container, had been powerful enough to kill.
"It shows that at this moment there are hotbeds of violence in Italian society that we have to confront," he told reporters.
No one immediately claimed responsibility for the attack.
It was carried out on the anniversary of Italy's 1945 liberation from Nazi German occupation and the remnants of Italian Fascist dictatorship at the end of World War Two.

Politicians from across the main spectrum said the choice of date and the timing ahead of Sunday's municipal elections in Milan and more than 1,000 other towns and cities appeared to be an act of intimidation.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi was due to visit the scene later on Friday.

The race for mayor of Milan is the highest profile contest in Sunday's elections, the biggest test of voter support since Prodi's centre-left Olive Tree coalition won a general election victory on April 21 last year.

The key candidates in Milan are incumbent Marco Formentini of the separatist Northern League, Aldo Fumagalli of the Olive Tree and industrialist Gabriele Albertini of Milanese media magnate Silvio Berlusconi's centre-right Freedom Alliance.

A run-off is likely on May 11 between the two top contenders from Sunday's poll with Formentini seen by many political analysts as risking defeat on the first round in what would be a blow to the League's prestige.

League leader Umberto Bossi, who has pushed an overtly secessionist agenda for northern Italy since the 1996 general election, broke with the mainstream view of the explosion, calling it a "centralist" bombing to scare voters off his party.
"It is a warning from thundering Jove to the sheep to make them stay in line," Bossi said.
Sunday's elections in Milan and elsewhere, including the large northern cities of Turin and Trieste, will be largely influenced by local concerns, according to analysts.
But they say political parties are bound to try to exploit the outcome for national advantage.

Prodi's government has faced popular resentment by inflicting tax hikes on Italians in its bid to help the country meet the tough budgetary criteria needed for membership of Europe's planned single currency.

The next step -- reform of the welfare state -- will be the most difficult, given resistance to spending cuts from the hard left party Communist Refoundation, which provides Prodi with his parliamentary majority, and from trades unions.
Berlusconi and other Freedom Alliance leaders told a rally in Milan on Friday that voters in the city should use Sunday's vote to try to oust the central government.
